speechtext: Omit the "freeze".

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend of the C.C.F. says "omit the freeze". I quite agree that my hon. friend from Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) have not said that you would have to impose a freeze upon wages and salaries to make a system of overall price controls effective. But what I am saying is that if we approach this subject with candour we will have to concede that the first step would have to be a freeze. You might not have to continue it, on the argument put forward by my hon. friends of the C.C.F.; but even on their argument it is conceded that a very substantial and, I venture to say, rigorous measure of control would have to be applied, even though you might ease the initial freeze on wages and salaries.
For myself I wish to make it as clear as I can that I am opposed to any freeze on wages and any freeze on salaries under present conditions or anything approaching present conditions. I wish to say further that, if it becomes a question of differentiating between a freeze and a substantial measure of control over wages and salaries, I am opposed under present conditions or conditions approaching present conditions to that rigorous control over salaries and wages which it seems to me my friends admit, or must admit, would be essential if any system of over-all price controls were to be attempted, in the hope of being made effective.
Either that rigorous control or that freeze, it seems to me, would have the effect of perpetuating many serious inequalities that exist today. In the field of wages there are all kinds of inequalities. So I come to one of the inherent weaknesses of this doctrinaire approach of laying down a flat program to meet present conditions. Present conditions are not so simple that they admit of any one simple expedient to meet them. The situation that parliament and the government face is infinitely complex, and you cannot meet it by introducing a simple program of overall price control such as has been advanced during this debate. Life is not constituted along simple lines like that. This whole complex structure that we call the Canadian economy is not constructed in as simple a way as that. Economic forces at work within that


widespread economy cannot be re-directed by measures as simple as that.
I have said something about wages. I wish to say something about salaries because I represent a great many white-collar workers. Broadly speaking, those white-collar workers have not had the advantage of the advancement in the returns that they receive from their hard labour that has attended the efforts of many wage earners to advance their position, both in respect of wages and working conditions, largely through the beneficent operations of collective bargaining through their labour organizations. The white-collar workers have not had that advantage, and as compared with many wage earners in this country who have had the advantage of collective bargaining and collective action their lot is worse, comparatively speaking.
To think today of imposing measures that would at the very least involve substantial and rigorous control of salaries would be, it seems to me, perpetrating a great injustice on tens of thousands of white-collar workers in this country. I for one am not prepared under present conditions, or under anything approaching present conditions, to subscribe to measures of rigorous control of the salaries of these white-collar workers, nor of the wages of wage earners. I am of the opinion that rigorous measures of that kind will do nothing but perpetrate inequities, exaggerate injustices that presently exist and create a measure of discontent that might easily approach a state of turmoil.
There is one other factor that I cannot forbear mentioning. I do not represent a rural constituency but I did have some experience with farm labour when I was a little younger.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: The hon. member has had experience in every field.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
No, I do not say every field, but I do mention the fact I have just referred to because I do not think every city dweller is as far removed from concern over the welfare of the farmer as perhaps some people are at times disposed to assume. We are told that the farmers of Canada want over-all price control. I do not doubt for a minute that many farmers would like to see the prices of many things controlled. I suppose every one of us if he gets down and talks from his heart of hearts will say, "Yes, I would love to see the prices of the things I have to buy controlled, not at the present high levels but to be rolled back. I would want to see them controlled at a very low level. But when it comes to things I have to sell, I do not want control."
At the very time that some hon. members in this house were speaking along those very lines I recall that representatives of the

Canadian Federation of Agriculture were before the government-just a fortnight ago- asking, not that the prices of farm produce should be frozen at present levels but should be increased. According to press reports the federation was asking for an increase in the price of domestic wheat; next, for the raising of the butter floor price and, next, for an increase in the floor price of bacon.
Let me make it quite clear-I think I can claim to be consistent in what I am saying- that I do not believe in freezing the returns which the wage earner is entitled to expect from his labour. Neither do I believe under present conditions in freezing the return to the white-collar worker for his labour. Similarly I do not believe that the returns to which the farmer is justly entitled as a fruit of his toil should be frozen. If you are going to start meddling with the forces of nature and the laws of economy then it seems to me that you must start here or there, and where will you draw the line? If you start with partial measures then of course you are going to create inequities, and every step you take will call for another in order to meet the inequities resulting from the last step.
The situation is just that, and I am afraid there is no escaping from it. If you are going to deal with it you have to go the whole way and clamp the tightest imaginable controls on the whole economy. I do not believe that the people of Canada are going to submit to the clamping of tight, rigid controls on the operations of the whole Canadian economy.
As one who has inveighed, I hope consistently, in the eight or nine sessions it has been my privilege to be a member, against the dangers of bureaucracy, I want to warn hon. members that the adoption of an overall rigid system will involve the re-establishment in this country of a bureaucracy that would be bigger than anything we have seen as yet, and which would take some time to put together.
We are not without recent experience as to the wisdom of the type of measures the government has been invited in certain quarters to take. Only several weeks ago the protagonists for the imposition of over-all price controls were pointing to the United States. They were saying that, as the United States had come to it, Canada must come to it. We have had more recent experience on this continent since those broad assertions were made.
The experience in the United States during the last month has been one of progressive decontrol, and the rate of progression
Emergency Powers Act has been rapid indeed. I saw figures the other day indicating that since the original freeze was put on a matter of five weeks ago some 200,000 articles have been removed from the effects of price control. It seems to me that anybody who can see in what is happening in the United States today a vindication of the argument that over-all price controls would be effective under present conditions, or under anything approaching present conditions, is simply closing his eyes to the facts as they have been unfolding themselves day by day in the United States.
Let me just say in conclusion that I concede at once the sincerity of my hon. friends of the C.C.F. in putting forth as they have year by year the same arguments as they are putting forward now. I will give them credit for consistency. Personally I think they have been consistently wrong, but I do give them credit for consistency. They can be consistent on this subject for a very obvious reason. As we Progressive Conservatives have been saying throughout recent years, the idea of control by the government over the economy of the country, of which price control with all its concomitant	controls is a leading
example, is	a	part	of	the mechanism ofsocialism. It	is	not	the	only mechanism ofsocialism. It	is	not	the	only expedient that
will characterize socialism in this country if such a time ever came when the people decided that they wanted socialism, but I say that this is one of the characteristics that will always attend socialism.
Therefore, believing as I do in the system of free enterprise, I do not approach this question at all with the same ideas as the socialists. They can afford to be consistent on this subject. For my part I choose to be consistent also in my opposition to the sort of things that they have been and are still advocating. I was not elected as a socialist, and it is no part of my business here, holding the views that I honestly hold, to try to out-C.C.F. the C.C.F.

When the C.C.F. brought in 'heir amendment two weeks ago I did not vote. No vote of mine in this house has been given to any doctrinaire subscription to what I think to be a program which will not work under present conditions. I do not say that

Emergency Powers Act the time will not come. I made that clear. I said that the system would work if we are faced with total war, if we are faced with more imminent aggression. Then we will unquestionably have to accept a greater measure of control over the economy.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It is not socialism at all. It is a matter of submitting, in the face of an emergency, to a form of control which I think the people will accept under conditions of total war, and I have no evidence that they are prepared to accept it under present conditions. There is an abundance of evidence to show that it will not work effectively unless there is almost unanimous support for it throughout the length and breadth of Canada. I do not want to see a system of that kind attempted to be imposed unless it is going to work, because if it were imposed and failed to work you would see a situation under which blackmarketing, as we saw it under the previous system, would simply pale away into insignificance alongside the extent of blackmarketing that would prevail under such conditions.
I have sought to be consistent. I have grave distaste for subscribing in any doctrinaire or dogmatic way to general programs that it seems to me assume a great deal. I think I have been thoroughly consistent in urging that parliament has no right, short of compelling necessity, to be giving to the cabinet extraordinary powers to do, while parliament is in session, things that parliament can do. Therefore it is with no enthusiasm, you may be sure, that I have seen this present measure, the emergency powers bill, accepted in the house, and have seen people urging upon the government that they not only accept these powers but go forward and use them at once and in a drastic form.
As long as this parliament is in session, as long as it is a free and sovereign parliament, I want to see it retain the right and function of taking those steps in the public interest that commend themselves to parliament as being necessary in that interest. I do not want to see parliament hand over such powers to any group of men no matter who they are. I do not care whether you have confidence in the government or whether you have not. I think it is inherently wrong, short of a condition of compelling necessity, for parliament to be handing over vast powers to the government to do, while parliament is in session, things that parliament is quite capable of doing.
Therefore I am not one of those who are telling the government to take these powers and to go rip-roaring ahead and use them. Rather I say to the government that I deplore
fMr. Fleming.)
the fact that they have come to parliament to claim, under this and other measures currently before the house, powers at the expense of parliament which I do not think parliament ought to be handing over to any government or any minister. While parliament is in session I want to see it retaining control of these situations, retaining the right to do the things that this supreme and sovereign parliament considers necessary in the public interest.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 115, to incorporate Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Could we have an explanation?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an act to incorporate Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company. The purpose of this company is to build an oil pipe line from the city of Edmonton in the province of Alberta to the city of Vancouver in the province of British Columbia via the Yellowhead pass. The proposed route is an all-Canadian route, and the pipe line will terminate in the city of Vancouver. It is proposed to build a pipe line of twenty-four-inch diameter which initially will carry oil at the rate of 75,000 barrels daily. The capacity may be increased by pumping pressure to an estimated 200,000 barrels per day. Marine terminal and storage
Private Bills
tanks will be built in the port of Vancouver for the shipment of that part of the oil delivered to that port which cannot be consumed in the province of British Columbia.
Important additions and extensive new refinery facilties can be envisaged as a result of the construction of this pipe line. I believe the members of this house would like to be assured that this is no frivolous application. It is not a proposal which suggests promotional aspects. The company that will build this line will be set up in Canada, and financed in Canada. The parent company is the Bechtel Corporation of San Francisco, the greatest pipe line building organization in the world today. One of the early achievements of this firm was the construction of the Hoover dam many years ago in cooperation with another group of contractors. For those who would care to study it, the history of this company was given great prominence in a lead article in Fortune magazine for the month of February. The Bechtel Corporation has over seven hundred engineers, and over five thousand offshore employees working on engineering projects in every part of the world. It has just completed a huge trans-Arabian pipe line-tap line as it is called. It has constructed a huge pipe line for the Pacific Gas and Electric Company from the state of Texas to the state of California, a distance somewhat in excess of 500 miles. Last year it completed in the Dominion of Canada 450 miles of our interprovincial pipe line. It now has under construction a thirty-two-inch pipe line from Kirkuk, in Iraq, across the Syrian desert, and the high Lebanon mountains to Banias on the Mediterranean sea.
Canadian contractors and Canadian materials will be used so far as possible. The total steel requirements, and this is a matter of major importance, have been arranged for, and construction is planned to begin in June of this year. It will be completed by the end of 1952. Associated with the Bechtel Corporation will be the oil companies supplying the oil which will flow through the pipe lines. Assurances have been received from the major oil producers that they will use this line to transport their products to the Pacific coast.
I should like to supply a few figures concerning consumption within the area that can reasonably be served by this pipe line when it is completed. The consumption of petroleum in British Columbia today is approximately 44,000 barrels per day. The state of Oregon, which is accessible to such a line, consumes 104,000 barrels per day. The state 'of Washington, which is easily accessible, consumes 130,000 barrels per day.

Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line The northern portion of the state of Idaho, which is the only portion which would be available to such a line, consumes something in the nature of 3,200 barrels per day. Shipment of the oil to Vancouver via this pipe line would mean additional revenue to Canada in 1953 of $50 million per year. Today on the Pacific coast we are spending our extremely precious United States dollars for petroleum products from the United States or South American countries which require United States exchange. This indicates that the saving to Canada would be very great, and it would increase in the ratio I indicated at the start as the volume of oil passing through the pipe line increases. To the British Columbian this is a distinct opportunity.
I am not without some knowledge of the economy of our province of British Columbia. I am going to say that nothing would serve us better than an integration of the economy of British Columbia with the economy of our neighbour to the east. We have a great many complementary products. I am going to say to my friends opposite, who sometimes have indicated this is a one-way traffic, that that is not the case. I would ask them to bear in mind that the people of British Columbia today obtain seventy per cent of the beef they consume from Alberta. Last year we brought in 930 carloads of Alberta potatoes. Of all the butter that we consume, eighty-two per cent comes from the province of Alberta. At the present time it may be interesting to note that we are consuming their eggs at the rate of $65,000 per week. If we could overcome the disadvantage of the great ribs of the Rocky range and could integrate our economies a little bit more closely, it would be of tremendous advantage to my province of British Columbia and, I am certain, to the province of Alberta as well.

speechtext: You are talking good sense now.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I want to indicate, if I may, some of the factors of production in the province of Alberta. I think we as Canadians too often overlook-and foreigners are not overlooking them today-the tremendous resources that exist in the province of Alberta. I think it could be well brought home to us that we have there resources that, if properly used, can be one of the great factors, if not the greatest, in the continuing prosperity and welfare of this nation. The figures I have are made available by the Stanford Research Institute which has done a great deal of work in the province of Alberta.	Incidentally, I think this is
a matter which could well go on the 

record of this house. I am informed by them or through them that the information they have obtained is most excellent, and that the officials and scientists employed by the province of Alberta and by the board in Alberta which is responsible for the maintenance of reserves there are of a nature of intelligence and foresight second to none among those with whom they have had to deal in any country in the world.
At the present time, effective January, 1951, the recoverable reserves of petroleum in the province of Alberta are of the nature of 1,250 million barrels of oil. That is the recoverable reserve, not the total reserve. The total reserve, based: upon 100 per cent, would be of the nature of 100 over 42 times this figure, because the recoverable reserve in Alberta averages out at 42 per cent of the total reserve. They vary from district to district from 25 per cent to 50 per cent, but on the average geologists are working on the assumption that the recoverable reserve is of the nature of 42 per cent of the total oil found in the ground. Accessions-that is, new discoveries-have been worked at the rate of 300 million barrels annually. So that we in that great province are finding additional oil to the extent of 300 million barrels annually of recoverable oil. If we project that into the future, we shall have in a few years a great increase in the recoverable oil from that area. It has been estimated that by January 1, 1953, there will be a recoverable reserve of 1,672 million barrels, notwithstanding the contemplated withdrawals, including the withdrawal taken out by this pipe line. So that we have in that area a tremendous value of oil.
I want to say a word or two, Mr. Speaker, concerning the importance of oil at the present time. We in the western democracies are faced with a tremendous threat to our institutions and indeed to our very lives. Of all of the aspects of defence, there is no greater strategy than the strategy of oil; because in our contemporary age, oil is power. In peacetime it is power to develop new industries, and power to transport people by land, by sea and by air. In wartime it is a vital necessity beyond any calculation. One-third of all the world's known reserves of oil lie within the United States. That is a most reassuring picture, but when you look at it more closely you find that the picture is not as reassuring as it seems at first blush. The estimated domestic production in 1949 was of the nature of 1,840 million barrels of oil; but this oil was drawn from 449,000 oil wells. The production worked out at 11 barrels per day only, which indicates that many of the United States wells are old, that they are over-exploited and that they are rapidly declining in production. Venezuela, which

had in 1949 a production of 457 million barrels of oil, produced that great quantity from 6,326 wells or an average of 201 barrels per day. The Middle East, which is one of the vital sources of oil at the present time, produced 512 million barrels of oil from only 208 wells, or a production of the nature of 5,500 barrels per well per day. When we give some thought to these figures we realize that we have an expendable reserve on this continent good for peacetime for twenty years. But when we say that we can foresee for that many years to come the requirements of oil in a peacetime economy, the picture is entirely changed if we think of war. If we could look forward to an assured period of peace, we would know what our oil would do. But under war conditions, when our safety and our security is threatened, there is simply no limit to be placed upon the immediate requirements of oil.
I was interested in seeing in the January issue of Foreign Affairs American Quarterly, attributed to a man by the name of Halford L. Hoskins, this most interesting extract:
Except for the promise of young Canadian fields, the outlook for long continued production in the fields certain to be available in time of emergency would be dim.
This again is a tremendous tribute to the resources which we have in the great province of Alberta. During the war, between 1940 and 1945, consumption of oil increased within the United States by the stupendous amount of 100 million barrels annually. Consumption in 1950 approximated 6,500,000 barrels of oil per day in the United States, which is, phenomenally speaking, two-thirds of the entire world production of oil.
The Middle East oil fields, which are today producing oil at the rate of 1,800,000 barrels per day for western Europe, are strategically extremely vulnerable. This oil is now going to western Europe and the wells are in a hazardous position by location. Transport is in an extremely hazardous position. As to oil, our security rests, to an uncomfortably large extent, upon ready supplies of oil. This proposed pipe line would take care of an eventuality where, through impairment of Middle East oil facilities, we could have Venezuela oil and California oil immediately drawn to Europe and could well be left without oil. It will provide an extremely valuable market for the growing production of the great province of Alberta. It will greatly increase the move toward1 the integration of the economy of our two great western provinces. We have heard lately in the house some discussion about distribution of industries across the country, and so on, and the necessity of bringing all parts of the country along. As a westerner I have felt that we 80709-62
Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line always like to think at least the great flanks of the country should be brought along economically with the same measure of progress as the central provinces. I think that the integration of the economy of our two most westerly provinces by the construction of such a pipe line as this would ensure that the western flank of this country would have prosperity for many years to come.
If the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is, as he was called yesterday, a sea lawyer, then I must say that I am probably a salt water petroleum engineer. In the short time that I have been endeavouring to study this question of oil I have found that it is the most engrossing story I have ever attempted to study. There are vast ramifications about it, and I could not hope to answer technical questions, and I do not think that hon. members would ask me to; but I will endeavour to answer some of the simpler questions if any hon. member would like to ask any afterwards.
I do want to thank hon. gentlemen for the attention that they have given me in the presentation of a project which I think ranks with the greatest projects in the Dominion of Canada at the present time.

As one of those who come from the province of Alberta may I say that this bill is important to us in that province for two reasons. First of all, we in that province are concerned in finding an outlet for our oil production. Every day new wells are being discovered, and every so often new fields are also being found. Therefore, it is important to us that we have an outlet for this oil or some outlet whereby we can dispose of it for marketing purposes.
This particular pipe line itself will not solve the problem. We need more pipe lines and immediately; that is why I should like to see this project go through.
The other reason is that I notice that this pipe line will go through the Yellowhead route. That is important, because it will tend toward the development of that particular area. It will certainly mean the construction of a better road. We have a road going through that pass now, but it will mean a better road in order to construct and maintain this pipe line. For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I am supporting this bill.

when the appropriate pipe line bill comes before the house I shall have plenty to say, particularly now that I know I have a champion to my right to assist me, in that he is committed to an all-Canadian route. The issue is this: I think it is admitted that there is only a market in British Columbia, Washington and Oregon for the oil that can be piped from Alberta by one pipe line. Will this oil pipe line which is to go to the Pacific coast pass through Canada to a Canadian port and be refined in Canada by Canadians, or will it go mainly

Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line through the United States to an American port where the oil will be refined by Americans? That is the issue at stake in the debates which will take place in the House of Commons on these oil pipe line bills.
As the house knows, the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) and I believe firmly in having a Canadian line, just as we did last year. All of the work will be done in Canada. We would certainly have to pay a higher price than if the oil were piped through an all-Canadian pipe line. It is very much to our advantage, and therefore to the advantage of the whole of Canada, to have this pipe line go through Canada rather than through the United States.

I believe most people are agreed that power is a commodity which should be developed and distributed by a public body. In Ontario we have the hydroelectric commission, and in practically every province of Canada today the development of hydro is publicly owned.
This is just another form of power; and power is so important to our whole economy that I think the people of Canada, through their own agencies, such as the Canadian National Railways, should consider the building of this pipe line-because, make no mistake about it, there is going to be only one pipe line. One can transport all the oil that will ever be used at the Pacific coast. Would it not be much better to have that pipe line owned publicly than to have it owned to a great extent by American capital?
I have no particular objection to the investment of American capital in this country; nevertheless I think it is unfortunate that the people of Canada themselves should not control their own basic resources. The only group in Canada able today to develop and build a pipe line is the government. We should be developing that pipe line; it should be built by the government, through one of its own agencies.
I appreciate that this pipe line is to be built through Canada, and that that is to be preferred to a pipe line going through the United States and then, after that country has been supplied, coming back up to our western coast. However, the fact that it is being built in Canada is one more reason why a government agency should be constructing it. In the first line of the bill we find the following:
Whereas an international emergency exists that threatens the security of Canada.
Emergency Powers Act
No one has denied the existence of such an emergency. There are high prices today. The purpose of this bill is not only to establish controls but to prepare this country for its defence. In that connection, and to answer the question put by the hon. gentleman, I believe that defence preparations in this country must start right now, so that we will not be caught by surprise if there is an enemy attack on Canada. It is for this reason that, although I am quite reluctant to do so, I will support the legislation which is now before the house.
I wonder what steps will be taken to improve the situation, and to establish a certain amount of control. What has happened in the United States can hardly be an inspiration for us. Government in this country is, I should say, better than it is across the boundary. It is easier to take control of a situation, even one which is as difficult as the one we now face. It is my sincere belief, sir, that we are facing an organized panic by reason of the well-known theory of Karl Marx concerning the struggle of the social classes. The propaganda must have been instigated by the same group of individuals who want to destroy the social standards of this country, and who take every means .at their disposal to create disorder. This is one of the main principles of communism. If one goes to the butcher or the grocer and sees the amount that is requested for food-well, he returns with an empty bag or buys a small quantity. It is well known. On the other hand, sir, how is it that not only every day but several times each day we have announcements in the newscast over the radio that the price of living is rising. Sometimes it has risen by a decimal, and sometimes by a point and a decimal. The figures may be accurate or otherwise. I cannot calculate the percentages in the cost of living index. I wonder how many people are employed in the dominion bureau of statistics to make that sort of propaganda throughout the country, and to give such a news item to the press agencies and to the radio networks of this country? When we know that the price we have to pay for everything, for clothes and for food, is high,

Emergency Powers Act what good is it to repeat that tact to the Canadian people three times a day? I will ask the government to take measures to fire all those fellows who make such calculations in the bureau of statistics. They are agents of Moscow, if not deliberately at least unwittingly. It is a part of a scheme to create trouble in the minds of the Canadian people when they have enough to worry about as it is.

I agree with the hon. member that parliament is supreme, but parliament sometimes takes a long time to act. This matter has been discussed for several days, and the bill has not yet passed. If the government is to get prepared for any emergency, let us start at once. The united front shall not be the front of the trade union leaders; it shall be the united front of parliament. Now that the members who differ from the government have expressed their views clearly, they must agree that, in virtue of one of the fundamental democratic principles, we must have the rule of the majority; we must abide by that. No supporter of any member who is doctrinaire will blame him for not having been diligent enough to expound his views here in the House of Commons on this matter.
It is my great pleasure to tell my hon. friends of all parties and groups in the house that they have made objective speeches and that they have spoken as faithful and welldeserving members of parliament. subtopic: PROVISIONS FOR ORDERS AND REGULATIONS DEEMED ADVISABLE FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not hold up the bill long,


nor do I propose to oppose it. As a matter of fact, I accept the Prime Minister's statement that the government has not now the necessary power to implement the controls which are necessary to meet the situation in which we find ourselves. We want parliament to grant that power to the government, and we want the government to use that power without delay in order to stop the rising cost of living. Whether the government chooses to use an over-all price freeze or, as the minister is reported to have said in a C.B.C. national broadcast, the government is considering a margin of profit control, or whatever other means the minister and his experts deem to be necessary to meet this emergency, we want those measures taken. Personally, I can see no great danger to our democratic institutions in the democratic procedure whereby parliament delegates power to the government and the government is responsible to parliament and to the country for its use of that power. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) this afternoon seemed to imply that that is socialism. I suggest to him that that is democracy at work in an emergency.
I do not like controls for their own sake, any more than does the hon. member for Eglinton; nor do I particularly like policemen. But I realize that without them my freedom would be jeopardized by someone who insists on doing as he pleases. There is a great deal of talk about personal freedom and about freedom of enterprise. I submit that intelligent freedom must recognize the right of the other fellow to some degree of freedom at least. Desirable as it may be, from the standpoint of those who make profits, to permit profits to rise, to permit certain combines to boost prices, to stockpile mpterial and thereby create artificial scarcities, the ordinary people have a right to some protection by the government against those prices. I can see no danger to our democratic institutions in granting that power democratically, through parliament, to the government for its judicious exercise.
As to the hon. member for Eglinton-as a matter of fact, I doubt if I would have had anything to say at this time except for some of his remarks-I said in a previous debate on this subject that the hon. member for Eglinton succeeded in balancing himself fairly well on the price-control fence. After listening this evening to him as he related all of the things that he does not believe in, and hearing little of what he believes in, I think I can conclude that he has at least come off the fence with regard to price control. It must be most refreshing to the Globe and Mail to learn that there is at least one good Tory left

in Ottawa, one Tory who follows the old traditional Tory policy and is still optimistic enough to believe that he can vie with the Liberal party for the support of big business in this country. A few days ago he applied the term "omnipotent" to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) or suggested that he should be given omnipotent power.

As to the hon. member's speech this afternoon, I thought he gave a good deal of evidence of belief in his own omniscience. He states, for instance, that controls cannot now work; and the proof that they cannot work is the fact that the hon. member for Eglinton says so. He states that the people will not support controls; and the only authority we have for that statement is that the hon. member for Eglinton said so. There is considerable evidence that the people of Canada would support the government at this time in measures of control necessary to curb inflation. I have already pointed out, as has been pointed out by others in the house, that the trade unions of this country have indicated their readiness to go along with the government and to co-operate with the government in the application of such controls as are necessary.
It has already been pointed out that public opinion polls have indicated that a great majority of the people in Canada would support these necessary controls. I do not think the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) is giving the Canadian people credit for being very intelligent when he suggests that everybody would want controls on those things that did not affect them; the farmers and others would not want anything that they were producing or had for sale to be controlled. I think the Canadian people as a whole today see the seriousness of the situation and that they would readily support the
Emergency Powers Act government in the adoption of and in the
application of necessary controls.
One of the arguments that the hon. member used was that prices are now too high; that they are at an all-time high, and it is too late to try to impose price controls. Well, if I recall correctly, the hon. member opposed price controls a year ago, when prices were not nearly as high as they are now, just as vigorously as he did this afternoon.
He admitted that price controls may be necessary in a period of total war. It is true we are not in the state of total war, but no one has criticized the government in this house more vigorously than the hon. member for Eglinton for not preparing for such an emergency. No one has indicated more vigorously that we may find ourselves in such a position without warning at almost any time. If such is a possibility, if it is true that we must prepare for such an emergency, and since no one disagrees with the statement that in such an event the government should have such powers, then I fail to see how we can logically oppose granting to the government at this time the powers that are necessary.
We must stop this merry-go-round sometime. Today's paper carried a report that two of the great labour leaders in this country, the heads of two of the greatest unions in this country, have already announced that their unions, representing hundreds of thousands of workers, will immediately ask for an increase in wages to offset the recent rise in prices. That just cannot go on indefinitely, and whatever steps are necessary should be taken by the government and without delay.
We have only to take up almost any paper today to find advertisers asking the public to buy now before prices go higher. The longer the government delays the worse the situation becomes. I suggest the government should be given that power; and furthermore, it should undertake to use that power by whatever measures are necessary.
There is just one further point to which I should like to call the minister's attention. In his broadcast reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail of this morning, he is quoted as saying:
Canadians could best help the defence effort and overcome inflation by refusing to buy anything unless it was an absolute essential.
I presume there are still some people in Canada, possibly a great many, who can buy non-essentials, but certainly with food alone for a family of four costing now, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, $22 a week, the ordinary people of this country just cannot afford to buy any non-essentials. It takes

When this matter was before the house approximately a month ago, Mr. Speaker, my colleagues, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) and the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) made our position abundantly clear with respect to price controls. In fact, sir, developments during the past month have convinced us that there exists a greater urgency today than existed a month ago for the government to take practical and realistic action toward meeting


this problem of the cost of living, which certainly has become an extremely acute problem as far as tens of thousands of our Canadian people are concerned.
This afternoon the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) seemed to build the greater part ot his argument around what he defined as a belief of his, namely a belief in free enterprise. I do not like the expression "free enterprise". I believe firmly in private enterprise under a set of conditions which will guarantee the survival of private enterprise. speechtext: I used both expressions.

speechtext:
The hon. member says he used both expressions. In my humble judgment, as a consequence of government policy we have departed so far from the laws of nature, as applied to Canada's economy-the laws of economy, whatever that might mean; and I am trying to give the definition which I believe the hon. member for Eglinton gave- that, as a result, today we are living under a set of conditions which are completely abnormal.
The present dangerous inflationary condition in my opinion results from two things. The first of these is what I would describe as certain rather stupid government policies pursued not only recently but at least for the last decade. Then, secondly, we all realize that this abnormal condition today has been aggravated by the necessity for the preparation of adequate defences to meet whatever dangers there may be in the near future.
This afternoon the hon. member for Eglinton capped his argument-at least, I assume that is what he thought he did-by referring to a statement made by a former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, at about the time of the conclusion of hostilities at the end of world war II. I would have been much happier if the hon. member had not made reference to Mr. Ilsley. He stated that the former minister had asserted that price controls would not and could not work in peacetime. But, as was pointed out in the house not so long ago by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. MARCH 6, 1951
Quelch), when in 1940 we made the suggestion that, owing to the rapidly climbing cost of living we should give consideration to some program of price controls, and rationing where necessary, it was the same Mr. Ilsley who said that it could not be done without a tremendous amount of bureaucratic control, and spying in every grocery store. However, it was only a short time after that that he was trying to convince the house, in effect, that he had been wholly and completely wrong, and that he could do it without any great amount of bureaucratic control and without putting a representative of the gestapo in every grocery store.
When price controls were debated in the house about a month ago the cost of living figure stood at 172.5. We pointed out, as did a great many other members in the house- possibly I should not say "a great many", but certainly a limited number-that today we have in Canada a body of about 238,000 old age pensioners who are finding it extremely difficult, if not in many eases virtually impossible to survive-and I use the word advisedly. Certainly many of them are obliged to get along without many of the things one would consider essential, such as certain necessary medical, dental, optical and other services. Of course in two or three provinces they would not have that problem, because in the three western provinces those services are provided.
Those people however are in a desperate position today. When I entered the House of Commons eleven years ago I believe they were receiving $20 a month as a basic pension. Today it is $40, if they are securing the maximum. That $40 today is of less value to them in meeting the cost of living than was the $20 they were receiving eleven years ago.
We have also that great body of workers who have not enjoyed increases in their incomes even remotely commensurate with the increase in the cost of living.
I shall mention another group-and I wish the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) were here, because I would say for his benefit that the wives and families of many servicemen today, those serving in the special force in Korea, are in many cases faced with serious difficulties in meeting the cost of living, plus those unavoidable hospital or doctor bills with which they are faced. Within the last few days I have received a number of communications relating to this matter.
Then of course we have the pensioners from the first and second world wars, and also a great many other people. We have tried to point out that this cannot fail to result in
Emergency Powers Act lower morale. We fear too that it is endangering the health of thousands of our people and we are most fearful that it could endanger our defence effort. We have pointed out several things which we think have contributed toward the present high cost of living. This talk about possible controls-controls if necessary, as it were, but not necessarily controls -is having a most damning effect. I have before me a file containing nineteen letters which were sent to a certain merchant within the past month by the suppliers of goods sold over his store counter. In all nineteen of these letters the suppliers have advised of immediate or pending increases in the prices of commodities they are supplying, such increases ranging up to as much as 25 per cent.
I am not going to refer to them in detail, but certainly the commodities listed are those which children must have every day. This talk about controls if necessary, but not necessarily controls, has caused many to hike their prices, in many cases I would say without justification, and in some cases with justification. But none of it justifies the circumstances which are leading them to have to do these things.
During the past month the wholesale prices for selected industrial and farm products have risen rapidly. Even at the time we were talking about this 172.5 cost of living index we had a positive guarantee, borne out by facts which could be observed by anyone, that there was bound to be a hike in the cost of living. I am going to venture the guess that if nothing more has been done before the end of this present year we are going to see a further minimum hike of anywhere from 15 to 20 points. I think I am extremely conservative when I say that, and I use the word conservative in its non-political sense.
Here is something else. Anyone who follows the financial publications knows that in many cases those engaged in business'-I am not saying all cases-have raised prices because of what they called uncontrollable factors, but right now they are declaring higher profits than they ever secured before. It is hard for me and for a lot of people to understand, much less appreciate, that sort of thing.

Sometimes I am rather dubious about what is governing their thinking, even though I have been here for quite a long time. What can we expect to happen? Should

Emergency Powers Act we continue to pursue the same policies, which are made up substantially of hope. What are we to assume may transpire? Is production of civilian goods going to shoot up suddenly and catch up with demand for some unexplainable reason? I think under existing circumstances one would have to be optimistic almost to the point of being foolish to think that that sort of thing could occur, especially with $5 billion expenditures for defence alone staring us in the face.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has told us and he has told the country that industry is operating at practically full capacity. He has told the house and the country that there are limiting factors in our export trade, such as supplies. He has told us and the country definitely that the full impact of the defence program has not yet been felt by the country. He has said that that defence program will definitely disturb our way of living. Does he mean a greater and greater and greater increase in the cost of living? If he does not mean that I should like to know what he does mean. He has said also, and we all know it, that there will be shortages.
All of that provides, with certain other things, the factors which have led to an increase in the cost of living of 2.7 points since the report of a month ago. When the housewife today goes to buy the commodities which are essential to the welfare of her family she finds that her dollar is worth approximately one-half of what it was worth ten years ago. If she goes to purchase certain things she will find that it is worth even less than that. In other words, to secure the same volume of commodities which she secured in 1939 she must have practically two dollars.
Let me tell you that there are plenty of Mrs. Browns and Mrs. Smiths, yes, and of Mrs. Shaws, who have not two dollars for every one dollar they had in 1939. What is the result? They buy possibly one-half the volume of commodities which they bought in 1939. Thus Mary and Johnny must get along with considerably less than they had in 1939 when the standard of living even then was not cracked up by welfare officers and others as being too high or even high enough in the light of the great productive capacity of this country.
If Mrs. Brown goes to the store today to buy certain groceries which I have noted here and if in buying them she thinks back just four years she will find that beef has- gone up about 141 per cent. She will find that veal has gone up about 111 per cent-I think actually the figures are higher because these are statistics of about a month ago-she will find coffee has gone up about 127 per cent; flour by about 78 per cent; milk by about 79

per cent; eggs by about 54 per cent; butter by 39 per cent and I notice another five cent hike today; sugar 45 per cent and bread, 67 per cent.
What we as members of parliament should do from the day we get home at Easter to the day we leave is to say to our wives, "You will not have to do any shopping while I am here, I will do it myself." I think many of us would come back wiser but possibly sadder men than we are right now. I think it would be an enlightening experience.
We have said, and I am going to repeat it, that we are convinced that government policy has proved its inability to meet and deal effectively with this problem of the cost of living. There has not been any evidence of it when you examine that cost of living index. While we do not like regimentation or the government meddling in the private affairs of our people any more than necessary, we believe that where the government has contributed so substantially toward the set of conditions which make action essential, if we are going to protect the welfare and health of our people, there will have to be some meddling by government temporarily.
We think there must be over-all price and wage control. We think that once the government has done that, even in spite of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), we will have gone a step toward solving the problem. I think there will have to be a quick freeze. I did not like the way the hon. member kept bringing out the word "freeze" all during his speech today. I am not going to suggest anything, but I think perhaps he was carried away by his own personal enthusiasm for what he was saying and did not know that he was using the word so often.
While some of us are advocating a quick freeze we realize that adjustments will have to be made immediately if fairness is to be the determining factor. We believe that after prices have been frozen there must be immediate adjustments to provide a fair profit. As stated by the hon. member for Acadia, we think that wages must go hand in hand with this. They have got to be frozen and then immediately adjusted to allow a fair return for the work done. Then we say that hand in hand with that we must establish our farm prices on a basis of parity. We consider it absolutely necessary that they be adjusted in the light of the new adjusted price level to be established. We think that every effort should be made by the government, and private business should be encouraged, to step up production in Canada. We believe that you are going to have to adopt consumer subsidies to meet the problem that

many persons in the extremely low income brackets are faced with today. We would even go so far as to say that in order to make that complete it would undoubtedly be necessary to ration certain commodities.
I know someone is going to say that is very strange for one who says he believes in freedom but, Mr. Speaker, if I were caught in a bear trap, before freezing to death I believe I would actually chew my own feet off. I think that much of my freedom, and I am afraid if this situation is allowed to go on without certain temporary drastic action such as I have suggested the net result can easily be the loss of our freedom.
In conclusion may I say that my reading has indicated to me that during world war I there was a Liberal government in Great Britain, and the prime minister and government of that day used to answer just about every question they were asked this way: Wait and see. I believe they even called the prime minister "wait-and-see Asquith", did they not? I wonder if what is happening in this country today is not a fair parallel of what existed over there.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is not very much that I want to say at this point. I am not rising to participate in the controversy between the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) andi the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). I think they are quite capable of handling that themselves, but there is one point that I think I should correct. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) seems to have got the impression from a speech I made a week ago that I had indicated that the government was unlikely to introduce any controls unless we got into something approaching an all-out war. I am sorry if anyone who heard that speech or saw a copy of it got that impression from it. I endeavoured to point out that there were many features in the present situation which resembled that of ten years ago, but there were also substantial differences. I did of course say that ten years ago we were in an all-out war and that we are not in an allout war at the present time.
Anyone who did not go beyond that might have gathered that in speaking about inflation, and the measures that would be appropriate to combat inflation, I had referred to an all-out war situation, but I was careful to point out-and I am sorry to have to refer to the language I used at that time-that I was not therein making an argument for or against controls. I pointed out that in 1941 the pressures bad developed to a greater degree in Canada than they had in the United States at that time because we had
Emergency Powers Act already been at war for two years and the United' States was not then at war. I pointed out that at the present time the pressures on prices and inflationary pressures generally seemed to have attained a greater degree in the United' States than they had in Canada, and that it was practically impossible to prevent some inflation in Canada when there was inflation in the United' States.
I boasted that the price controls we had introduced in 1941 had operated in a very satisfactory and successful way, and that for that reason it might appear to many that what had been successful then would be successful now. I also added that I was very sorry that I could not feel that was so because if we did feel that by the introduction of price controls we could cure this situation we would be very happy to adopt them. Then I put the question: "But is that so?" I then went on to discuss what seemed to me to be substantial differences between the situation of that period and the situation of this time.
I did say that at this time we were trying to build up our strength as rapidly as possible to prevent the outbreak of a third world war, whilst in 1941 we were in the throes of an actual war, and were cutting out all but the bare essentials and devoting the whole of the rest of our energies to the winning of that war as quickly as possible.
I said that while building up the required strength to deter war we wanted to be able to maintain a fair standard of living, to maintain our standard of living at a reasonable level. I added that, in other words, we did not want to cut our civilian standard to bare essentials unless and until we have to, but I certainly did not intend to convey the idea that there was nothing to be done unless we were in something approaching all-out war.
I said that the government might of course hold down the prices of our imports because the commodities we import at this time are a much greater proportion of our consumer goods than those that were being imported in 1941. At that time we were importing only the things required for the prosecution of our war effort while at the present time we are importing larger quantities of civilian commodities, the prices of which depend upon the markets from whence they come. I said that we could keep the price of these imported commodities down by subsidies, but that we did not know to what extent the controls that were being attempted in the United States might be successful, and that if we entered upon a policy of that kind we did not know what the extent of the drain on our own treasury for subsidies might become.

Emergency Powers Act
I also pointed out that the prices of the consumer goods of the classes of our exports were very much dependent upon the prices that could be obtained in the markets to which they were exported, and that that had to be so because if we fixed ceilings that were below the prices that could be obtained in the markets to which our exports went all these commodities would go to those markets unless they were embargoed and we compelled the producers here to sell them to Canadian consumers at prices lower than those that could be obtained in the foreign markets. I said that if anything of that character were attempted there would have to be equalization pools established to give a substantially similar return to all producers of the total quantity.
I also said that it was true that we had kept prices below the United States price level between 1941 and 1946 but that our price ceilings did not prevent a considerable measure of wartime inflation. What they did was to alleviate and postpone the effect of that wartime inflation, but once the war was over we found it was not practicable to have a price structure seriously out of line with the price structure in the United States, and we had to allow our prices to catch up. I added that I thought it had been a wise policy to postpone the effects of inflation until the war was over and until we could devote our energies to the production of greater quantities of commodities for civilian purposes; that would help to meet this problem of inflation. I stated that it was wise to remember that our price ceilings had not prevented inflation, and I ventured to make the bald statement that price control by itself cannot prevent inflation. What it can do is to change the direction and retard some of the effects of inflation. Then I said that, of course, is not an argument either for or against price control.
I went on to say that we must try to keep as low as possible the amount of commodities taken off for our defence purposes, and to see to it that the remainder left for civilian consumption was distributed as fairly as possible, and that price controls [DOT] might help to do that, but that we would be deceiving ourselves if we thought price controls gave us the whole answer. Then I added that another serious problem in connection with price controls was the matter of enforcement. During the war there was this patriotic urge that made us accept the restrictions or inconveniences to which we were being subjected without too much murmuring, because we all realized that they were quite inconsequential when compared with what our brothers, our sons and daughters in the

armed forces overseas were doing for the country. This created a situation in which most of us here felt that the price control and rationing system was operating in a manner that was fair to everybody, and that was necessary for our own salvation. It would be difficult to obtain that kind of public support for price controls at the present juncture, and no one in this country would want the kind of controls that can only be enforced in a police state.
Then I went on to say that all this does not mean that some controls are not being considered. We have some already, and parliament is at the present time dealing with a bill to give the government power to impose wider controls. We will not hesitate to impose any controls we believe will really work to protect our people generally against the injustice of rising prices. But we are not going to recommend controls unless and until we can honestly tell the public we believe they will work. We are not going to do any shadow-boxing merely because it might get us some immediate applause. At the present time, we do not feel that the conditions are such that an over-all system of price control would be really effective. We wish it were otherwise, and it may become otherwise; and as I said earlier we are keeping our minds free and ready to adapt our policies to any new and changing conditions.
We are asked to declare at this time what the government's intentions are. The government is in the position where, if it declares its intentions, they must not be intentions merely designed to serve for the production of paving blocks for the nether regions. They have to be the kind of intentions we believe we can carry out and implement. Some hon. members seem to believe that price controls at this time would cure the situation. I do not think they would. I do not think it would be healthy for a democratic government to give the impression that it was going to put into effect a series of restrictions on the freedom of the citizens, unless it also coupled that with the assertion it believed it was something that was going to work and which would, in the end, prove to be beneficial to the welfare of the community.
Some reference was made to questions that were put to my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) by gentlemen of the press last night. Some questions concerned whether we were considering a mark-up or profit control. We are having all those matters examined, and we are endeavouring to find what we can do that will prove to be effective. There are a great many who believe that it can be done at once by price

control, but not everyone believes that. When I returned from Quebec, where I had the privilege of spending the week end, I found a letter from the Canadian Association of Consumers, signed by the president, Mrs. Dorothy L. Walton. There was a note on it saying she had sent copies to the leader of the opposition, the leader of the C.C.F. party and the leader of the Social Credit party. The letter contains this statement:
The C.A.C. feels that the establishment of over-all price ceilings is not a safe answer to the price problem at the moment. It considers, moreover, any kind of control that might be set up for prices must include controls on the ingredients that go into prices, and that wages and salaries form an important part of such ingredients.
I do not know Mrs. Walton. I inquired, and I was told that this was a large representative association of Canadian housewives who have been considering this problem, and that is their conclusion. The situation the government faces is that some inflation has been inevitable. Hon. members say that we did not, through the Bank of Canada, put restrictions upon the extension of credit as quickly as we should have. There may be something in that reproach, but at the present time those restrictions have been applied. The governor and administrators of the Bank of Canada are, I feel from my contacts with them, as concerned over the validity of Canadian currency as any of us. They have been watching the situation carefully, and we have not just been waiting to see, but we have been listening to their advice and endeavouring to adopt measures which we thought would be proper to recommend to the Canadian public as things which we believe, in spite of the inconvenience they might cause certain members of the public, to be for the general welfare of the whole people.
I must confess that there is some small measure of truth in the assertion that there are members on this side of the house who have been urging that price controls be resorted to at once. One of them said to me, "Well, even if we are not confident they will work, why don't we just try them to let the people see they do not work? After all, you never know what will work until you try it". That reminded me of a little jingle I heard a long time ago which runs like this:
I wonder, quoth the maiden with a sigh:
Could I look in my ear with my eye?
I am sure I could do it If I put my mind to it;
You never know what you can do till you try.
I was not convinced that we had to go quite that far, and try things that appear obviously to us to be like attempting to look into one's ear with one's eye. But that does
Defence Production Act not mean, and I would not want anyone to take it, that I am indicating that the government is unlikely to impose controls unless and until we are in something approaching all-out war. We will, just as quickly as we can find reasonable grounds to believe in the efficiency of any or all controls, not hesitate to use the powers provided by this bill, if and when it receives the assent of the two houses of parliament and of the representative of His Majesty.
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
Agreed.

I am sorry that that amendment is not acceptable to the government. In the first place, how in the world could you define what part of the business is involved? There is no chalk line drawn around a particular operation. The reason that a controller is put in charge-and it is the only reason-is that the management of the plant is inefficient. If the management were proper, there would be no need for a controller. I remember the appointment of some twenty or twenty-five controllers during the course of the last war, but I cannot remember an occasion on which a controller was put in to control only part of a plant. The controller is put in to control the management of the plant so that it can carry out its obligations. The difficulty may be that the plant is in bankruptcy through inefficient management or the situation may be that the plant is keeping false accounts. But in any case I do not see how you could apply the duties of a controller to part of the plant and not to all of the plant. The thing would be a farce. We would spend 

endless time trying to get a decision as to what part of the operation was involved, when the whole operation was undoubtedly involved. Of course if you had a plant in one city and a plant in another city, you could then put a manager into the plant which was working on the contract, straighten out the management of that particular plant, and allow the other plant in which you were not interested to do what it liked. That can be done. But that is an exceptional case. Usually the plant is an integrated plant and the management applies to all the operations.

speechtext: I appreciate the point of what the minister has said; but by using the word "plant" and overlooking the fact that the wording of the section and the wording of the amendment is "business", I think he has missed the point I was trying to get at. In that case it would be easy to say, and the decision would be upheld, that the whole of the plant was necessarily involved in the performance of the contract. But here we have used the word "business". I am sure there must be many cases in which concerns operate plants in separate cities or where one side of their business perhaps is engaged in a manufacturing process and the other side is engaged in a distributing process but it is the same business and may be the same company operating both processes. What this amendment is designed to ensure is that the powers to appoint a controller would be limited only to the side of the business which is engaged in the manufacturing under the defence contract, and that if the distributing process was not necessarily involved in the performance of that contract or compliance with the direction, then there would be no power to extend the authority of the controller over that distributing process. Dear Mr. Garson:
I am in receipt of your letter of the 2nd instant enclosing proposed amendments to the British North America Act respecting old age pensions and a provincial sales tax. I have also received your further letter of the 20th instant.
With reference to the amendment to section 95, it is suggested that the words "or the legislature of any province" be added after the words "the parliament of Canada" where they occur in line 2 of subsection 2 of section 95 of the proposed amendment.
You will recall that the Prime Minister indicated that there would be concurrent legislation with respect to old age pensions and therefore the amendment should not be placed in section 91 of the British North America Act. In view of the wording of subsection 1 of section 95, and in order that there should be no question but that the legislatures of the provinces will have concurrent jurisdiction and will be enabled to enact legislation dealing with the age group of sixty-five to seventy and possibly to supplement the dominion old age pension at seventy, it seems to me that it is necessary to incorporate these words in the proposed amendment; otherwise the courts might construe the section as giving exclusive jurisdiction to the dominion, which I am sure you will agree was not intended.
The amendment to head 2 of section 92 as submitted appears to incorporate the agreement made at the Ottawa conference, and I have no objection to the addition of the words "and not so as to discriminate between sellers or classes of sellers of the same class of goods" as proposed in your letter of the 20th instant.

Dear Mr. Garson:
Your letter of January 3 enclosing drafts of two constitutional amendments to deal with old age pensions and retail sales tax, together with your letter of January 20 suggesting certain additional words to be inserted in the draft with regard to sales tax, have received careful attention in cabinet council. I am therefore writing to inform you of the conclusions which we have reached.
Your suggestion is that the question of old age pensions should be dealt with by adding a new subsection to section 95 of the B.N.A. Act. You will recall that during the discussion of this subject at the conference I made the proposal that old age pensions should be dealt with as a new subsection of section 91. We would like to repeat that suggestion now.
Under the proposal which is now before us, the federal government will be assuming complete responsibility for pensions to persons aged seventy and over and fifty per cent of the cost of pensions to persons aged sixty-five to sixty-nine inclusive. The result will be that the total cost to the federal treasury will be somewhat of the magnitude of $356 million while the total cost to all ten provinces will be approximately $32 million. In other words, the federal government has indicated its willingness to assume more than 90 per cent of the financial costs of old age pension schemes. Under these circumstances it seems to us fundamentally unsound that we should continue ten separate provincial administrative organizations in the field of old age pensions, each one of them overlapping with the federal jurisdiction and each one of them requiring constant exchange of information and constant co-ordination of information and administrative practices. On the grounds of eliminating unnecessary duplication of administrative machinery and of avoiding frequent misunderstandings between different governments, it is our view that one central uniform administrative machinery should be created to deal with the question of old age pensions. For this reason we would strongly urge that the proposed amendment with respect to old age pensions should simply be the addition of a new subsection in section 91 which would read "old age pensions."
If, however, this proposal does not find favour with your government and with the governments of the other provinces, we are prepared to support an amendment which will authorize the federal government to deal with old age pensions while continuing the authority of the provinces to do likewise. We feel, however, that there may be certain confusions created if the proposed amendment is made a subsection of section 95. At the present time section 95 follows a heading which reads "Agriculture and Immigration." It will obviously be somewhat misleading to carry under that heading a subsection dealing with old age pensions, and it may therefore be necessary to amend the heading also or to set up the proposed amendment as a separate section rather than as a subsection of section 95.
We understand that pensions for the blind are to be brought under the same arrangements as are proposed for persons seventy years of age and over. We therefore submit that the constitutional amendment in connection with old age pensions should have added to it the following: "and to pensions for the blind."
We have also given consideration to the proposed amendment to section 92, head 2, which would change that head so as to read as follows:
"2. The raising of revenue for provincial purposes by
(a) direct taxation within the province, and

(b) indirect taxation within the province in respect of the sale of goods (except goods sold for shipment outside the province) to a buyer for purposes of consumption or use and not for resale, at a rate not exceeding three per centum of the sale price, but not so as to discriminate between sales of goods grown, produced or manufactured within the province and sales of goods grown, produced or manufactured outside the province and not so as to discriminate between sellers or classes of sellers of the same class of goods."
This proposed amendment deals only with the sale of goods. It would therefore presumably not apply to such things as electrical power, or services provided by laundries, theatres, hotels, restaurants, barber shops and the like. It was our understanding that this amendment should enable the province to impose this type of tax wherever it is a more convenient method of raising revenue from the people in the province who get the benefit of goods and services available in the province. It therefore seems to us that the proposed amendment should make it clear that it covers these other types of industries which provide services directly to the consuming public.
Our advisers have suggested that since the proposed amendment, in prohibiting discrimination between sales of goods local to the province and those from outside the province, makes no specific mention of goods manufactured partially outside and partially inside the province, it might be possible to evade the prohibition by discriminating either against or in favour of goods partially manufactured within and partially without the province. Your government may desire to provide against any such possibility.
Yours very truly,
Douglas Campbell

In our view the main and overriding purpose of such an amendment is to be found in the advantage which would accrue to the provinces through being
able to impose such indirect taxation in lieu of a purchasers' or consumers' tax such as is now found in five of the provinces. In at least two of these, including our own, the existing tax rate is in excess of three per cent. In the light of this situation we can see no advantage to be gained through a constitutional amendment which would limit or restrict a province in the manner suggested.
We would strongly urge that the federal government amend its proposals to permit the imposition of a tax at a higher level; to meet our situation it should be at least four per cent.

Premier's Office Saskatchewan
Regina, February 10, 1951
Hon. Stuart Garson, K.C.,
Minister of Justice and Attorney General,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Garson:
Attached please find copy of our "Routine Proceedings" of February 8, in which you will note the resolutions which I placed on the order paper and which will probably be discussed and dealt with in the course of the next few days.
I thought you would be interested in having this, lest there should be any question raised as to the position which Saskatchewan takes with reference to the two constitutional amendments which your government has suggested.
Yours sincerely,
T. C. Douglas
Extract from Routine Proceedings and Orders of the Day of the legislative assembly, province of Saskatchewan, No. 6, Thursday, February 8, 1951. "Government Motions
1.	Hon. Mr. Douglas (Weybum), to move the following resolution:
That this assembly approves in principle the amendment of section 95 of the British North America Act, as proposed by the government of Canada, following the federal-provincial conference held in December 1950, under which, notwithstanding anything contained in the said act, the parliament of Canada may make laws in relation to old age pensions.
2.	Hon. Mr. Douglas (Weyburn), to move the following resolution:
That this assembly approves in principle the amendment of section 92 of the British North America Act as proposed by the government of Canada, following the federal-provincial conference of December 1950, under which, in addition to the power already possessed by the province, the province shall have power to raise revenue for provincial purposes by:
'Indirect taxation within the province in respect of the sale of goods (except goods sold for shipment outside the province) at a rate not exceeding three per centum of the sale price, but not so as to discriminate between sales of goods grown, produced or manufactured within the province and sales of goods grown, produced or manufactured outside the province, and not so as to discriminate between sellers or classes of sellers of the same class of goods.' ''

Premier's Office Prince Edward Island
Charlottetown, March 2, 1951
Hon. Stuart Carson., K.C.,
Minister of Justice,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Garson:
Thank you for your letter of February 28, regarding proposed constitutional amendments.
The position of the government of Prince Edward Island regarding these amendments is that contained in my letters to you of January 5 and 25 last.
Should, however, it become expedient to adopt one of the substituted draft amendments set forth in your letter of February 28, respecting old age pensions, Prince Edward Island would prefer the text of the third draft.
Yours very truly,
J. Walter Jones Premier
Wednesday, March 7, 1951	MISCELLANEOUS PRIVATE BILLS
